## **ORDER** 

The present Petition is filed by the Petitioner, M.P. Power Management Company Ltd. (MPMCL), for seeking payment of the balance outstanding amount of Rs 83.229 crore by the Respondent, UP Power Corporation Ltd (UPPCL), along with interest (in compliance with the decision in MoM dated 9.8.2018) pertaining to Rihand and Matatila Hydro Power Station. 

**==> picture [20 x 20] intentionally omitted <==**

_Order in Petition No. 320/MP/2022_ 

_Page_ _**1** of_ _**3**_ 

## **Background** 

2. Rihand (300 MW) and Matatila (30 MW) Hydel Stations were commissioned in 1966 and 1965, respectively. As per the agreement dated 09.01.1963, UP was required to supply 15% of the power from Rihand and a one-third share from Matatila to MP due to the submergence of land in MP. Since disputes arose regarding nonsupply of power and compensation, MP filed Petition No. 107/2007 before the Commission. The Commission, vide order dated 12.11.2008, directed UPPCL to pay compensation to MP, which was upheld by APTEL vide judgment dated 21.07.2011 in Appeal No. 151/2008. Subsequently, disputes regarding Rajghat HPS and compensation were also adjudicated by the Commission. Thereafter, APTEL, in Appeal Nos. 59/2014 and 120/2014, directed both States to explore amicable settlement of disputes. Pursuant thereto, and in compliance with the decision recorded in the MoM dated 09.08.2018, a settlement was arrived at whereby UPPCL was required to pay Rs. 157.782 crore to MPPMCL in instalments. However, UPPCL paid only Rs. 74.553 crore, leaving a balance amount of Rs. 83.229 crore unpaid, which led to the present dispute. 

3. The Petition was admitted on 13.04.2023, Subsequently, the matter was listed for hearing on 10.08.2023, 10.10.2023, 21.2.2024, 02.07.2025, 12.08.2025, 26.09.2025, 27.11.2025, and 18.03.2026. During the hearing on 10.10.2023, the Commission directed the parties to explore the possibility of a mutual settlement of the issues. 

4. The Petitioner vide affidavit dated 15.5.2026, and the respondent vide affidavit dated 14.5.2026, have submitted that the issues involved in the present petition have been mutually settled between the parties and have requested that the present petition be dismissed as withdrawn. 

**==> picture [20 x 20] intentionally omitted <==**

_Order in Petition No. 320/MP/2022_ 

_Page_ _**2** of_ _**3**_ 

## **Hearing dated 27.05.2026** 

5. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that an affidavit has been filed confirming receipt of the due amounts from the Respondent. The learned counsel for the Respondent submitted that the matter stands settled and that affidavits to this effect have been filed by both parties; the extract of the same (Petitioner) is given below: 

_“in compliance to MoM dated 06.11.2024, a meeting was held through video conferencing on 04.08.2025 between the Director (Corporate Planning), UPPCL and CGM (Regulatory), MPPMCL to amicably settle the issues involved in the present litigation and to give effect to the Minutes of Meeting dated 09.08.2018 signed 25.07.2018 in Appeal no. 59 of 2014 and Appeal no. 120 of 2014. Consequent to the above, a mutual consensus has been reached where UPPCL agreed to pay Rs. 83.21 Cr. (subject to cross verification) to MPPMCL in 4 monthly instalments from October, 2025 onwards. Accordingly, UPPCL has made the payments against the instalments decided earlier_ .” 

6. In view of the above submissions, the present Petition is disposed of as ‘withdrawn’. 

7. Petition No. 320/MP/2022 is disposed of in terms of the above. 

**Sd/Sd/Sd/Sd/-**

In response, the learned counsel for the Petitioner strongly opposed the prayer of IEX for the impleadment and submitted that the matter being regulatory in nature did not need the intervention of a third party. The learned counsel also submitted that IEX had no locus standi in this case as it was not in any way an aggrieved person.

11. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, the Commission reserved the Petition as well as IA for order.

12. We have considered the submissions by the Petitioner and the Intervenor, IEX. The present Petition has been filed by the Petitioner seeking the grant of time to one of the promoter shareholders, namely PTC, to dilute its stake in the Petitioner Company to meet the requirements/ compliance under Regulation 15 of the PMR 2021. However, before dealing with the above aspect, it is necessary to first decide on the application filed by IEX, seeking impleadment as a party Respondent in the present Petition and permission to file its reply.

without any application, and on such terms as may appear to it to be just, direct that any of the following persons may be added as a party: (a) any person who ought to have been joined as plaintiff or defendant, but not added; or (b) any person whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the court to effectively and completely adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit. This Commission is vested with a similar discretion by virtue of Regulation 37 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission ( _Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023_ . However, it is equally trite law that if a person is not found to be “a proper party” or “a necessary party”, the court does not have jurisdiction to order his impleadment against the wishes of a Plaintiff. A “necessary party” is a person who ought to have been joined as a party to the suit and in whose absence an effective decree cannot be passed by the court. Whereas a “proper party” is a person whose presence would enable the court to completely, effectively and properly adjudicate upon all the matters and issues, though he may not be a person in favour of or against whom a decree is to be made. As regards the ‘necessary party’, neither any relief has been prayed against IEX, nor is it the case that no effective order can be passed in the present case in the absence of IEX. Hence, IEX cannot be considered a necessary party. Similarly, we are unable to see how the presence of IEX is required for a complete, effective, and proper adjudication of the matter/issue involved in this case, i.e., the relaxation of the provisions of the PMR 2021 to consider it a proper party.

14. Even in its application, IEX has not made out any case as to how it is a necessary party or, at least, a proper party to the proceedings. All that has been submitted is that the Petitioner, under the guise of Power to Relax, is seeking permission to act contrary to the provision of the PMR 2021, and that too without impleading the other exchanges and affording an opportunity of hearing and representation, particularly when at the stage of the authorisation specific undertaking was given by the Petitioner pursuant to the specific objections being raised. It is

also submitted that IEX has complied with the relevant regulation by having one of its clients surrender its ‘client’ status on its platform within the required timelines under the PMR 2021, and it would be prejudiced if the present Petition is allowed by the Commission. However, these submissions do not in any manner justify IEX being a proper party to this Petition. Whether the Petitioner has made out any case for relaxation of the provisions of the PMR 2021 for grant of time to PTC for diluting its stake to meet the requirement/compliance under Regulation 15 of the PMR 2021 needs to be examined on its own merits. A competing exchange cannot claim an opportunity of a hearing or making representation, as a matter of right, on the ground of being a proper party to such proceedings. Also, the prejudice averred by IEX does not appear to be a prejudice against any direct or legal interest but merely a commercial interest. In view of the above, we find that IEX is neither a necessary nor a proper party to these proceedings and its application for impleadment is therefore liable to be rejected.
